title: What is a sargable (Search-ARGument-ABLE) predicate, and why does wrapping an indexed column in a function (`WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026`, `WHERE DATE(ts) = ...`, `WHERE UPPER(email) = ...`) defeat a normal index range scan — how do you rewrite it as a range (`created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2027-01-01'`) or use a function-based/expression index, and why should you confirm the fix with the execution plan rather than assuming the index is now used?
shortTitle: What is a sargable predicate, why wrapping an indexed column in a function defeats a range scan, and how to rewrite it

s1_definition.profdef: A sargable (Search ARGument ABLE) predicate is one the optimizer can satisfy by seeking directly into an index, because the indexed column appears bare on one side of the comparison and is compared to a constant or a range. Wrapping the indexed column in a function, applying arithmetic to it, or forcing an implicit cast makes the predicate non-sargable: the engine must evaluate the expression per row, so it cannot use the index's natural ordering and falls back to a full scan. You restore sargability by rewriting the function predicate as a half-open range on the raw column, or by creating a function-based (expression) index that matches the exact transformation.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India ledger index is sorted by the raw created-at timestamp. A sargable question is "give me everything from 1 January 2026 up to but not including 1 January 2027" — the clerk opens the index at the first date and reads a clean range. A non-sargable question is "give me everything where the YEAR of the date equals 2026" — now the clerk must compute the year of every single row before deciding, because the index is sorted by full dates, not by extracted years. Same answer, but one lets the clerk use the sorted shortcut and the other forces reading the whole ledger.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep the indexed column bare and compare it to a range — the moment you wrap it in a function, the index range scan dies.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A sargable (Search ARGument ABLE) predicate is one the optimizer can satisfy by seeking directly into an index, because the indexed column appears bare on one side of the comparison and is compared to a constant or a range. Wrapping the indexed column in a function, applying arithmetic to it, or forcing an implicit cast makes the predicate non-sargable: the engine must evaluate the expression per row, so it cannot use the index's natural ordering and falls back to a full scan. You restore sargability by rewriting the function predicate as a half-open range on the raw column, or by creating a function-based (expression) index that matches the exact transformation.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India ledger index is sorted by the raw created-at timestamp. A sargable question is "give me everything from 1 January 2026 up to but not including 1 January 2027" — the clerk opens the index at the first date and reads a clean range. A non-sargable question is "give me everything where the YEAR of the date equals 2026" — now the clerk must compute the year of every single row before deciding, because the index is sorted by full dates, not by extracted years. Same answer, but one lets the clerk use the sorted shortcut and the other forces reading the whole ledger.

**One line to remember:** Keep the indexed column bare and compare it to a range — the moment you wrap it in a function, the index range scan dies.

sections.s2_technical:
An index is a B+tree sorted by the raw column value. A seek works by navigating to a starting key and walking a contiguous range of leaves. For that to be possible the column must appear untouched so the engine can map your comparison onto the sorted keys. `WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2027-01-01'` is sargable: the engine seeks to the first key on or after the lower bound and stops at the upper bound.

`WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026` is not sargable because `YEAR()` transforms each stored value; the index is sorted by full timestamps, not by extracted years, so there is no contiguous key range to seek. The same applies to `WHERE DATE(ts) = '2026-05-01'`, `WHERE UPPER(email) = 'X'`, `WHERE balance + fee > 1000`, and `WHERE SUBSTRING(account_id,1,3) = 'SAV'`. In every case the engine computes the expression for all rows, which is a full scan.

The first and best fix is to rewrite as a half-open range on the raw column. `YEAR(created_at) = 2026` becomes `created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2027-01-01'`. `DATE(ts) = '2026-05-01'` becomes `ts >= '2026-05-01' AND ts < '2026-05-02'`. Using a half-open upper bound with strictly-less-than correctly includes the last instant of the day and avoids boundary bugs with timestamps.

When a rewrite is not possible — for example a genuine case-insensitive email match — the second fix is an expression index that stores the transformed value: `CREATE INDEX ix_email_lower ON accounts(LOWER(email))`, and then the query must use exactly `WHERE LOWER(email) = ?` so it matches. The transformation in the query and the index must be identical.

A senior nuance: implicit type coercion silently causes non-sargability. Comparing an indexed `VARCHAR` account id to a numeric literal, or an indexed `BIGINT` to a quoted string, can make the database cast the column instead of the literal, defeating the index. You fix it by matching the literal's type to the column. The final and most important nuance is verification: after any rewrite you must run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` and confirm the plan now shows an Index Scan or Index Range Scan, because an expression index that does not exactly match the query, or a leftover cast, will keep the scan and you would never know without the plan.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The year-end tax report runs `WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026` over two hundred million transactions and takes minutes, pinning the database CPU. This is exactly a non-sargable function predicate; rewriting it as a half-open date range restores the index range scan.

Problem 2 — The daily settlement query uses `WHERE DATE(settled_at) = CURRENT_DATE`. This also strips sargability; the fix is `settled_at >= today AND settled_at < tomorrow`.

Problem 3 — Login genuinely needs case-insensitive email matching and cannot avoid a transformation. This is exactly where a function-based expression index on LOWER of email is the right tool, as long as the query uses the identical expression.

The mini-project builds a reporting service with a non-sargable method, its sargable range rewrite, and a case-insensitive login backed by an expression index. It logs each rewrite and reminds the engineer to verify the plan.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build and run
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/sargable-service-1.0.0.jar --spring.profiles.active=dev

# BEFORE: non-sargable → Seq Scan (confirm, do not assume)
psql -d bankdb -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE EXTRACT(YEAR FROM created_at)=2026;"

# AFTER: sargable range → Index Scan using ix_created_at
psql -d bankdb -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM transactions
  WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2027-01-01';"

# Expression index → confirm it is actually chosen
psql -d bankdb -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE LOWER(email)=LOWER('rajesh@bank.in');"
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the tax team wants every 2026 transaction. The naive query is `WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026`.

Step 1 — The naive query asks the engine to compute the year of `created_at` for each of two hundred million rows. The index `ix_created_at` is sorted by full timestamps, not by extracted years, so there is no contiguous range to seek and the planner picks a sequential scan.

Step 2 — The service rewrites the request to a half-open range: `created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2027-01-01'`. The column is now bare and compared to constants.

Step 3 — The planner maps the lower bound onto the sorted index, seeks to the first key on or after 1 January 2026, and walks the leaves forward.

Step 4 — It stops the instant a key reaches 1 January 2027, because the upper bound is strictly less-than. TXN001 dated March 2026 is included; TXN002 dated January 2027 is correctly excluded.

Step 5 — The engineer runs EXPLAIN ANALYZE and sees "Index Scan using ix_created_at," confirming the fix actually took effect rather than assuming it did.

```text
2026-10-25 14:25:05 INFO  TaxReportService - Sargable range: created_at >= 2026-01-01T00:00 AND created_at < 2027-01-01T00:00 (uses ix_created_at)
2026-10-25 14:25:05 INFO  TaxReportService - Case-insensitive email via expression index ix_email_lower
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A sargable predicate, short for Search ARGument ABLE, is one the database can satisfy by seeking directly into an index because the indexed column sits bare on one side of the comparison and is matched against a constant or a range. An index is a B-tree sorted by the raw column value, so the engine can only seek when it can map your comparison onto that sorted order. The moment you wrap the column in a function, do arithmetic on it, or trigger an implicit cast, the predicate becomes non-sargable: the engine has to evaluate the expression on every row, and the index range scan collapses into a full table scan.

That is exactly why WHERE YEAR of created-at equals 2026, or DATE of a timestamp equals a day, or UPPER of email equals a value, all defeat a normal index. The index is sorted by full timestamps or raw emails, not by extracted years or uppercased strings, so there is no contiguous key range to walk. The primary fix is to rewrite the function predicate as a half-open range on the raw column: created-at greater than or equal to the first of January and strictly less than the first of the next January. The strictly-less-than upper bound cleanly includes the last instant and avoids timestamp boundary bugs. When a rewrite genuinely is not possible, such as case-insensitive email matching, I create a function-based expression index and make sure the query uses the identical transformation.

At the National Bank of India our year-end tax report was written with YEAR of created-at, and over two hundred million transactions it pinned the database CPU for minutes because it scanned the whole table. I rewrote it as a half-open date range and it dropped to a fast index range scan. For the login path, which truly needs case-insensitive matching, I added an expression index on LOWER of email and matched the query to it.

The habit I never skip is verification. After every rewrite I run EXPLAIN ANALYZE and confirm the plan now says Index Scan rather than Sequential Scan, because an expression index that does not exactly match the query, or a stray type cast, will quietly keep the scan, and the execution plan is the only honest proof that the fix actually worked.
